title: Stop trusting your AGENTS.md: the drift-check that makes it a contract
author: Veaceslav
summary: Back in September I published Stop bloating your AGENTS.md: reference your conventions instead of pasting them — and advice I still stand behind: keep AGENTS.md a thin index, move the details into per-topic docs, reference them from one place. The argument was about context hygiene — your conventions stay detailed, your context stays clean. What that argument never claimed to do was enforcement. It was a solid argument. It was also half an argument, and the second half bit me within two weeks of real agent work. Because here's the uncomfortable truth I glossed over: a lean AGENTS.md is still just prose. ESLint enforces boundaries because CI turns red. AGENTS.md enforces itself because... nothing does. The agent reads it, nods, and the next time a task touches an edge case the doc doesn't cover, the doc becomes fiction. It doesn't drift loudly. It drifts quietly, one merge at a time, until you open it a month later and realize it describes a codebase that doesn't exist. So this article is the missing half: how I turned AGENTS.md from advice the agent reads into a contract CI can enforce — the eval-suite moment from part 4 of the JobCopilot series, but for the doc that runs the project. And per house rules of this series, I'm leading with the ways it broke, not the ways it worked. 1. The lie we tell ourselves: "the doc is enforced because it's true" Before the fix, the honest inventory of what my "lean" doc could guarantee: Lint boundaries — enforced . CI. Type checks — enforced . CI. "New scenario UI goes in src/features/<feature>/ui/ , never app/ " — suggested . "Never commit to main" — enforced-ish, by branch protection, but invisible in the doc. "Use pnpm only" — suggested , until a second lockfile quietly appeared. The pattern is: everything tooling can express gets enforced; everything that needs a sentence of prose gets vibes. And agents read prose the way juniors read style guides on Friday afternoon. The fix wasn't writing more prose. The fix was giving every sentence of prose in that doc an ID and a hook that a script can execute. 2. Give every rule an address: <!--check: id --> The doc now looks like this (real shape from the repo, trimmed): ## Package manager <!--check: single-lockfile --> This repo uses pnpm ONLY. pnpm-lock.yaml is the single lockfile. A second lockfile (package-lock.json, yarn.lock) in the repo = CI red. ## Data <!--check: no-ui-fetch --> src/features/ **/ui/** and app/ ** must NOT call fetch/axios directly. Data access belongs to feature logic. Two design decisions worth pausing on: The marker sits next to the rule, not in it. The prose stays human-readable; the marker stays invisible in rendered Markdown. Whoever edits the doc — human or agent — sees the rule, not plumbing. Every rule carries a check marker, and every marker is mapped. If a rule appears in the doc without a marker, it's a suggestion. If a marker exists but no check is implemented, that's not a TODO — it's a bug: somebody thought they'd promised the machine something . The one sentence that made this work: "If CI is red, fix the code OR the rule — never bypass the check." Both directions are legitimate edits. Silencing the check is not. 3. The drift-check: a doc that can fail like a test The checker is a small Node script — pure Node, no shell tools, because the repo has to verify identically on Windows, Linux and CI. Core of the real file, abbreviated (the npm-era shape — story 3 below renames these ids to cmd-pnpm-* ): import { readFileSync } from " node:fs " ; /** AGENTS.md text — the contract being verified. */ const md = readFileSync ( " AGENTS.md " , " utf8 " ); /** Rule ids from <!--check: id--> markers, de-duplicated, in document order. */ const ids = [ ... new Set ([... md . matchAll ( /<!--check: \s * ([\w - ] + )\s *-->/g )]. map (( m ) => m [ 1 ])), ]; /** Map: AGENTS.md rule id -> verification function. Return contract: true = pass, false = generic fail, string[] = offending files. */ const checks = { /** package-lock.json present — npm is the real package manager. */ " cmd-npm-install " : () => existsSync ( " package-lock.json " ), " cmd-npm-lint " : () => hasScript ( " lint " ), /** UI layers must do no direct fetching. */ " no-ui-fetch " : () => { const bad = [... hits ( " app " ), ... hits ( " src/shared/ui " ), ... featureUiHits ()]; return bad . length ? bad : true ; }, }; // Two-way binding: doc -> map, and map -> doc. for ( const id of ids ) if ( ! ( id in checks )) problems . push ( `rule ${ id } has a marker but no check is mapped` ); for ( const id of Object . keys ( checks )) if ( ! ids . includes ( id )) problems . push ( `check ${ id } exists in the map but no marker in AGENTS.md` ); Then every rule runs, and any failure exits 1. On a green repo the whole suite takes under a second: ✓ AGENTS.md OK: 11 rules verified · 0.0s And when things drift — rename a mapped file, add an unmapped marker, plant a fetch in a UI file, all exit-1 cases we actually reproduced in the first week: ✗ rule some-new-rule has a marker but no check is mapped ✗ drift detected: 1 rule(s), 1 binding issue(s) Since this series lives in Python, here is the same two-way-binding loop as a ~25-line Python twin — the logic is the point, not the language: import re from pathlib import Path # Every rule in AGENTS.md carries an HTML marker next to it. MARKER = re . compile ( r " <!--check:\s*([\w-]+)\s*--> " ) md = Path ( " AGENTS.md " ). read_text ( encoding = " utf-8 " ) # de-duplicated, in document order ids = list ( dict . fromkeys ( MARKER . findall ( md ))) # Your map: rule id -> function that returns True / list of offending files checks : dict = {} # {"single-lockfile": ..., "no-ui-fetch": ...} problems = [ f " rule { i } : marker in AGENTS.md, no check mapped " for i in ids if i not in checks ] problems += [ f " check { c } : exists in the map, no marker in AGENTS.md " for c in checks if c not in ids ] print ( f " AGENTS.md: { len ( ids ) } rules " ) for p in problems : print ( f " ! { p } " ) raise SystemExit ( bool ( problems )) Fed a real 11-rule AGENTS.md with an empty checks map it exits 1 with eleven "no check mapped" lines — exactly the failure you want the first time you wire the markers in. Same discipline as the part-4 evals: the contract has an exit code. In fsaa-next it runs as its own GitHub workflow — .github/workflows/agents-md.yml, triggered on [pull_request, push] — parallel to ci.yml. The doc stops being advisory. 4. What broke in practice The part I promised. Four failures, in the order they were discovered. 1. The parser eats itself. I wrote a doc section explaining the marker system and — being an idiot — pasted a literal example: "add a marker like <!--check: my-rule --> ". The regex found it, treated my-rule as real rule #12, two-way binding flagged it, suite red. The doc's explanation of the contract violated the contract. Fix: explanations in the doc must never contain a live marker; paraphrase. (The irony was noted and savored.) 2. The check that green-lit too easily. The first version of the import-boundary rule checked whether eslint.config.mjs contained the boundary config — the words, not the effect. The rule was checking the check, not reality: relax or mangle the ESLint rules and the drift-check stayed green while actual cross-slice imports crept in. The rewrite scans the real files for real imports that shouldn't exist ( @features/ inside src/shared/ , upward imports anywhere), and keeps the config-word check as a second, independent guard. Lesson that cost the rewrite: a check can inspect the enforcement, which is not the same as inspecting the code. Always ask what the worst violating diff looks like — and whether your check catches that , or merely catches a keyword. 3. The package-manager migration nobody scoped. Switching npm to pnpm broke three things, and only one of them was on my list: (a) pnpm/action-setup@v4 conflicts with an explicit version: input when packageManager is pinned in package.json — red in 4 seconds on every push; (b) the old npm ci sitting in ci.yml, a different file, easy to forget; (c) the drift-check's own rule ids, still named cmd-npm-* . Three files, one decision. What saved it from becoming permanent archaeology: the contract rules ( single-lockfile , cmd-pnpm-* ) were updated in the same PR as the migration — because the contract lives next to the code, the PR diff itself shows all three. 4. Rule rot — the doc version of drift. A refactor renamed app/layout.tsx ; the file-paths check went red on the next run, before anything downstream noticed. That's the quiet win of the whole setup: the contract fails exactly like a test nobody had time to write. 5. Verdict: is this overkill? For a weekend project — yes, probably. Lean prose gets you 80% of the value, and I'll defend that in the next "bloat" debate. But the 20% gap is where agents live. Every convention not expressible as CI is a convention an agent will eventually violate with total confidence, generating a code review you then do by hand. The drift-check replaces that review with an exit code. On an 11-rule contract it costs a few hundred lines of boring Node/Python and one workflow file — cheaper than a single forgotten lockfile incident. The honest revision of my September advice: keep AGENTS.md lean, reference your conventions — and then make every remaining sentence falsifiable. A rule that nothing can break isn't a rule; it's a suggestion the next agent will politely decline. JobCopilot returns next week, with the graph wiring and the negative-test story. If an AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md of yours has gone quietly fictional, I want that war story — comments open. Follow if you want the rest of the series. title: Where the 150 seconds actually go: profiling a local render loop
author: mujin
summary: I generate on a 4GB GTX 1650, SD1.5 in fp32 with model offload. One 512x768 image takes about 150 seconds. That number is useless on its own — it tells me nothing about what to change. So I timed the loop in pieces. Splitting the 150 seconds into model load, sampling steps, and PNG encode The first version is a stopwatch and a cProfile dump, wrapped around the three phases I care about. It fits in a screen: import cProfile , pstats , time , io from PIL import Image def timed ( pipe , prompt , seed , out ): t = {} t [ " load " ] = time . perf_counter () pipe . enable_model_cpu_offload () t [ " load " ] = time . perf_counter () - t [ " load " ] t [ " sample " ] = time . perf_counter () img = pipe ( prompt = prompt , width = 512 , height = 768 , generator = torch . Generator (). manual_seed ( seed )). images [ 0 ] t [ " sample " ] = time . perf_counter () - t [ " sample " ] t [ " encode " ] = time . perf_counter () img . save ( out , format = " PNG " ) t [ " encode " ] = time . perf_counter () - t [ " encode " ] return t pr = cProfile . Profile () pr . enable () t = timed ( pipe , prompt , seed , " out.png " ) pr . disable () print ( t ) pstats . Stats ( pr ). sort_stats ( " cumulative " ). print_stats ( 15 ) On my card the split comes out roughly as: model load and offload setup takes a noticeable slice, sampling dominates, PNG encode is small but not zero. I am not going to quote a breakdown I did not log per-phase — what matters is that the stopwatch gives you three numbers instead of one, and cProfile names the function inside the dominant phase. What the profile changed Two fixes actually cut wall-clock: One: stop reloading the model. The load phase was being paid every run because the script was re-entered fresh. Keeping the pipe alive across the loop and only offloading weights between calls removed the repeated setup cost from every image after the first. Two: fix the sampling call, not the sampler. The cumulative profile put the time inside the denoise loop, which is expected. The real change was making the loop's inputs stable — same resolution, same step count, no per-call resizing — so the offload pattern stopped thrashing between CPU and GPU. The 150 seconds is the floor I accept at 512x768 fp32; I stopped trying to shave the loop itself and started removing everything around it. The "optimization" that only moved cost to disk: caching intermediate latents and re-encoding. cProfile stopped attributing time to sampling and started attributing it to file writes. Wall-clock barely changed. I reverted it. If a change moves time from the sampler to the disk without lowering the total, it is bookkeeping, not speed. The single per-run number worth writing to a file Per image, append one line: seed, wall_seconds, phase_split . That is it. Not loss, not step count — wall seconds and where they went. The reason is the 77 pieces I generated and pinned. At one line per run, a slow week shows up as a drift in that column before I have to guess why. If the sampling phase grows, it is the loop or the hardware. If load grows, it is the environment. If encode grows, it is the disk. One number, three phases, and the trend is visible without a session of re-profiling. The rest of the pipeline — the ERC-721, hand-built Seaport listings, the restock daemon, the fact-gated copywriter, the ~271-test suite — does not need this number, but the render loop is the only part I cannot make faster by writing better code, so it is the only part I measure every run. The collection this feeds is live at https://thunderous-sunflower-a910b4.netlify.app — 7 of 77 minted, 70 to go, 5 per wallet, mint at 0.00063 ETH on Base, preload about 0.0000008 ETH per piece. Takeaway for today: add a one-line CSV append to your render loop that records wall seconds per phase. It costs a few lines and turns "why was this week slow" into a column you can read.

title: I built a hash map from scratch (and now I know why dictionaries are fast)
author: Leandros Georgiou
summary: In Python, if you have a dictionary with a million things in it, my_dict["apple"] still comes back instantly. I'd use dictionaries for ages without knowing how that's possible, so as part of my data structures project I built my own version from scratch, called a hash map. Here's how it works. The problem with a list Let's imagine we stored our pairs in a normal list: fruit = [[ " apple " , 1 ], [ " pear " , 7 ], [ " fig " , 2 ]] To find the value for "fig", we have to check "apple", then "pear", then "fig". With three items that's fine, but with a million items we might have to check a million. This is O(n): the more items there are, the longer it takes. A hash map gets around this by not searching at all. It works out exactly where the key should be and goes straight there. Hashing: turning a key into a position Python has a built-in function called hash() that turns a value into a big number. The important thing is that the same key always gives the same number while the program is running. That number is far too big to use as a position in a list, so we use % (the remainder) to squash it down to fit. If we have 8 slots: index = hash ( key ) % 8 This always gives a number from 0 to 7. So "apple" might always go to slot 3. When we want "apple" back later, we do the same calculation, get 3 again, and look straight in slot 3. No searching through everything. One thing that surprised me: if you print hash("apple") , you get a different number every time you restart Python. That's done on purpose, for security. But it stays the same while your program is running, which is all a hash map needs. Buckets Each slot is called a bucket, and each bucket is just a list. So the whole hash map is a list of lists: self . buckets = [[] for _ in range ( capacity )] There's a trap here. You might think you could write [[]] * capacity instead, but that makes one empty list and puts it in every slot, so all 8 "buckets" are actually the same list. Put something in bucket 3 and it shows up in every bucket. The version above makes 8 separate empty lists. Collisions There's a catch. There are loads of possible keys but only 8 buckets, so sometimes two different keys land in the same bucket. This is called a collision. For example, whole numbers hash to themselves in Python, so with 8 buckets: hash(0) % 8 = 0 hash(8) % 8 = 0 0 and 8 both go in bucket 0. That's why each bucket is a list, so it can hold more than one pair. Bucket 0 would look like this: [[ 0 , "zero" ], [ 8 , "eight" ]] So when we look for 8, we go straight to bucket 0, then check the few pairs inside it. That's still really fast, because a bucket only has a handful of pairs in it, not the whole map. The code Here's the main part of my hash map. _index works out the bucket, set stores a pair, and get finds one: def _index ( self , key ): return hash ( key ) % self . capacity def set ( self , key , value ): bucket = self . buckets [ self . _index ( key )] for pair in bucket : if pair [ 0 ] == key : # key already here, so update it pair [ 1 ] = value return bucket . append ([ key , value ]) # new key, so add the pair self . size += 1 if self . size / self . capacity > 0.75 : self . _resize () def get ( self , key ): bucket = self . buckets [ self . _index ( key )] for pair in bucket : if pair [ 0 ] == key : return pair [ 1 ] raise KeyError ( key ) Notice, get only ever loops through one bucket, never the whole map. If the key isn't there, it raises a KeyError , just like a real dictionary does. Resizing Collisions are fine when the buckets are short. But if we kept adding pairs to 8 buckets, say 1,000 pairs, every bucket would have about 125 pairs in it, and we'd be back to slow searching. So the hash map keeps track of how full it is. This is called the load factor: load factor = number of pairs / number of buckets When the load factor goes over 0.75, the map doubles its number of buckets and puts every pair back in again. Why put them all back in? Because the bucket a key goes in depends on how many buckets there are. Remember, 8 went in bucket 0 when there were 8 buckets. With 16 buckets: hash ( 8 ) % 16 = 8 Now it belongs in bucket 8. Therefore, every pair has to be worked out again and moved to its new bucket. Resizing takes a while, because it touches every pair, which is O(n). But it only happens now and again, and because the map doubles each time, it happens less and less often. Spread out over all the set calls, adding a pair is still O(1) on average. So why are dictionaries fast? Putting it all together: Hashing means you jump straight to the right bucket instead of searching. Buckets handle collisions, so two keys can share a slot. Resizing keeps the buckets short, so checking a bucket stays quick. That's why getting, setting and deleting are O(1) on average, no matter how big the map gets. Python's real dictionary is cleverer than mine about collisions (it doesn't keep a list in each slot), but the big idea is the same: hash the key to go straight to the right place, and grow before it gets too full. Testing it I wrote pytest tests for it, including putting 1,000 keys into a map that started with only 8 buckets, to make sure it resized properly and could still find every key. I also tested a collision on purpose (0 and 8), and that asking for a missing key raises a KeyError . The full code and tests are in my repo: data-structures-from-scratch

title: How to Export Public Telegram Channel Posts to CSV (Text, Views, Dates, Links) Without an Account or API Key
author: frankxie
summary:
A lot of public information appears on Telegram first. Exchanges post listings and delistings there, projects announce releases, and news channels push stories before the website updates. If you research a market or monitor a competitor, you will eventually want those posts in a table: one row per post, with the text, date, view count and links. The official routes are awkward. The Bot API only sees channels where your bot is an admin. The full MTProto API (Telethon, Pyrogram) works, but needs a Telegram account with a phone number, an api_id from my.telegram.org and a session file to keep safe. That is a lot of setup for posts anyone can already read at t.me/s/<channel> in a browser. This tutorial uses an Apify Actor that reads that public web preview and exports the posts as JSON, CSV or Excel. Disclosure: I built and maintain this Actor. It is a paid tool ($1.00 per 1,000 results). The limitations section at the end is as important as the rest. What you can do with the data Monitor announcement channels. Pull 30 days of an exchange's channel and tag each post: delisting, new listing, maintenance, promotion. Compare channels. Views per post, posting frequency and hours, and which sites they link to. Build a research dataset. Original-language text with dates and engagement, ready for topic or sentiment analysis. Step 1: Set up a run in Apify Console Open Telegram Channel Scraper and click Try for free . The input form has these fields: Field What it does What to scrape ( mode ) posts (posts of channels), search (posts that contain a keyword) or channelInfo (one row per channel, with subscriber count and description). Channels ( channels ) Public channels as names ( durov ), @names ( @durov ) or links ( https://t.me/durov ). Search keyword ( searchQuery ) Only for search mode. Max results ( maxItems ) Upper limit for the whole run. You're only charged for saved results. Max posts per channel ( maxItemsPerChannel ) Stops one busy channel from using up the whole run. Only posts newer than ( postedAfter ) A date like 2026-10-01 or a period like 7 days . The Actor stops reading a channel when it reaches older posts. Single post links ( postUrls ) Optional links like https://t.me/telegram/105 if you only need specific posts. No Telegram account, phone number, API key or proxy is needed. Step 2: Run it and export Click Start . When the run finishes, open the Output tab and export as JSON, CSV or Excel. For this article I ran this input, the newest 10 posts each from Binance's announcement channel and Telegram's own news channel: { "mode" : "posts" , "channels" : [ "binance_announcements" , "telegram" ], "maxItemsPerChannel" : 10 , "maxItems" : 20 } It finished in about 4 seconds and saved 20 posts. Here are two of them. I removed the textHtml field, the media list (long file links) and most empty fields to keep this short; the values that remain are unchanged. Both are public brand channels, and none of these posts had an author signature, so there was nothing personal to redact: [ { "type" : "post" , "channel" : "binance_announcements" , "channelTitle" : "Binance Announcements" , "messageId" : 9089 , "url" : "https://t.me/binance_announcements/9089" , "text" : "Notice of Removal of Spot Trading Pairs - 2026-10-30 


 Based on our most recent reviews, Binance will remove and cease trading on the following spot trading pairs: 
 - At 2026-10-30 03:00 (UTC): AAVE/BTC, ATOM/BTC, CAKE/BTC, DASH/BTC, ETC/BTC, ICP/BTC, PENDLE/BTC, RENDER/BTC, TAO/BTC, THETA/BTC, XAUT/BTC and XTZ/BTC 

 👉🏻 Learn more here" , "postedAt" : "2026-10-27T08:31:38Z" , "views" : 20700 , "isEdited" : false , "mediaTypes" : [ "photo" ], "mediaCount" : 1 , "links" : [ "https://www.binance.com/en/support/announcement/detail/de45689cbd7b4e1fa87055cdf5a85997?utm_source=EnglishTelegram&utm_medium=GlobalCommunity&utm_campaign=AnnouncementBot" ], "hashtags" : [], "mentions" : [], "reactionsTotal" : 93 , "reactions" : [ { "emoji" : "❤" , "count" : 35 , "isPaid" : false , "customEmojiId" : null }, { "emoji" : "🤔" , "count" : 26 , "isPaid" : false , "customEmojiId" : null }, { "emoji" : "👍" , "count" : 16 , "isPaid" : false , "customEmojiId" : null }, { "emoji" : "🤯" , "count" : 8 , "isPaid" : false , "customEmojiId" : null }, { "emoji" : "👏" , "count" : 5 , "isPaid" : false , "customEmojiId" : null }, { "emoji" : "🙏" , "count" : 3 , "isPaid" : false , "customEmojiId" : null } ], "scrapedAt" : "2026-10-27T21:24:28Z" }, { "type" : "post" , "channel" : "telegram" , "channelTitle" : "Telegram News" , "messageId" : 453 , "url" : "https://t.me/telegram/453" , "text" : "350 Million GIFs. The GIF panel now contains over 350 million GIFs in 36 languages. 

 Your Telegram GIF searches are entirely private and do not rely on any third parties. 

 July Features 
 1 • 2 • 3 • 4 • More" , "postedAt" : "2026-07-19T17:58:17Z" , "views" : 2020000 , "isEdited" : false , "mediaTypes" : [ "video" ], "mediaCount" : 1 , "links" : [ "https://t.me/telegram/450" , "https://t.me/telegram/451" , "https://t.me/telegram/452" , "https://t.me/telegram/454" ], "hashtags" : [], "mentions" : [], "reactionsTotal" : null , "reactions" : [], "scrapedAt" : "2026-10-27T21:24:28Z" } ] Even 20 rows show a few patterns. The 10 Binance posts covered five days, and all of them went out within two minutes after the hour or half hour (07:02, 08:01, 08:31, 09:01 UTC and so on), which looks scheduled. The 10 Telegram posts came from two feature drops, in July and August, each posted as a burst of messages within a minute or two. Telegram's channel shows no reactions, so reactionsTotal is null there, not zero. links holds every link in the post, including ones hidden behind text like "Learn more here". Step 3: Do it from Python Install the official client and pandas: pip install apify-client pandas Then pull the last 30 days of one channel and save a flat CSV: from apify_client import ApifyClient import pandas as pd client = ApifyClient ( " YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN " ) run = client . actor ( " pipiagent/telegram-channel-scraper " ). call ( run_input = { " mode " : " posts " , " channels " : [ " binance_announcements " ], " postedAfter " : " 30 days " , " maxItems " : 2000 , }) items = list ( client . dataset ( run . default_dataset_id ). iterate_items ()) df = pd . DataFrame ( items ) # Flat columns for the CSV; nested lists like media and reactions are easier to use from JSON. cols = [ " channel " , " messageId " , " postedAt " , " views " , " reactionsTotal " , " text " , " url " ] df [ cols ]. to_csv ( " binance_announcements_30d.csv " , index = False ) Now tag and summarise the posts. Some posts have no text or no reactions, so the code handles missing values: df [ " postedAt " ] = pd . to_datetime ( df [ " postedAt " ], utc = True ) text = df [ " text " ]. fillna ( "" ). str . lower () categories = { " delisting " : r " removal|delist|will remove " , " new listing " : r " will list|new trading pairs|will support " , " maintenance " : r " maintenance|upgrade " , " promotion " : r " competition|campaign|rewards?|giveaway " , } df [ " category " ] = " other " for name , pattern in categories . items (): df . loc [ df [ " category " ]. eq ( " other " ) & text . str . contains ( pattern ), " category " ] = name summary = df . groupby ( " category " ). agg ( posts = ( " messageId " , " count " ), median_views = ( " views " , " median " ), median_reactions = ( " reactionsTotal " , " median " ), ). sort_values ( " posts " , ascending = False ) print ( summary ) # Posting hours (UTC) print ( df [ " postedAt " ]. dt . hour . value_counts (). sort_index ()) # Which sites the channel links to domains = df [ " links " ]. explode (). dropna (). str . extract ( r " https?://([^/?]+) " )[ 0 ] print ( domains . value_counts (). head ( 10 )) The patterns are a starting point for this one channel; adjust them after reading a few dozen posts. To monitor a channel, schedule the same input in Apify with "postedAfter": "1 day" and append each run's results to your table. De-duplicate on channel + messageId , because runs can overlap. What it costs You pay per saved result: $1.00 per 1,000 results , with no start fee and no monthly rental. A post with an album of ten photos is still one result. The 20-post test above: $0.02 30 days of a channel that posts about 10 times a day (around 300 posts): about $0.30 Channel info (subscriber count, description) for 50 channels: $0.05 You can set a maximum charge per run in the run options, and the Actor stops when it reaches it. Limitations These mostly come from what Telegram shows on its public web preview: Public channels only. Private channels, invite links ( t.me/+... ), groups, bots and user accounts can't be read. They are skipped with a warning in the log. Some public channels have no web preview. Owners can turn it off, Telegram hides some restricted channels, and a channel blocked in the country of Apify's servers looks like it doesn't exist (a proxy can help). No comments. Comments under posts aren't part of the web preview. Views and reactions are rounded by Telegram above 1,000 ("20.7K" becomes 20700), so small differences between posts don't mean much. Views keep growing after a post goes out. In my sample, Binance posts from four days earlier had more than twice the views of the newest ones. Compare posts of similar age, or re-run later. Some post types show no content on the web. Live streams, giveaways and paid media come back with empty text and a mediaNote . Media links expire. The Actor saves links to photos and videos, not the files. Download them soon if you need them. Search returns at most about 22 posts per channel and keyword. For more, scrape the channel's posts and filter them yourself, as in the example above. Old posts take time. The Actor reads newest to oldest at roughly 1,000 posts a minute. Personal data. Author signatures and forwarded-from names can identify people. If you store them, make sure you have a legitimate reason under GDPR or similar laws. If you track many channels, run channelInfo mode daily to build a subscriber history. The store page has more input examples. If something doesn't match what this article says, open an issue there and I'll look into it.

title: AI made building easy. So where's your moat?
author: Richard Kersey
summary: Building in public, part 2: how to find the thing an auto-completer can't copy Originally published on Chirpper . Anyone with an AI coding tool can rebuild your product over a weekend. That's not a fear anymore, it's just true. So the question every builder has to answer now isn't "can I build it?" It's "what still protects me after someone copies it?" This piece gives you a way to answer that for your own project. I'll use the day I asked the same question about my own social site as the worked example, including the part where I got it wrong. The day I asked the question On March 5, 2026, I started designing a social site with ChatGPT. The idea: no logins, and posting only by invite. Every invite links back to whoever sent it, so your reputation travels with the chain of people who brought you in. A few prompts in, I stopped and asked the scary question: "What's the moat? If it's simple to build are we already dead - I don't think so - cause this is more like a first mover advantage play where no one could copy it once a network effect is created." In the same message I named it. I already owned chirpper.com, so that was that. The answer I got back is the framework below, plus what almost eight months of actually running the thing taught me about it. What stopped being a moat Start by crossing these off. They used to buy you time. With AI writing most of the code, they don't anymore. Your code. If it can be described, it can be rebuilt. A tight spec is basically a copy button. Your features. A feature list is a prompt someone else hasn't typed yet. Your UI. Screenshots are enough to clone a design. Shipping first. Being first only helps if being first leaves something behind that a later arrival can't get. That last one is the key. First-mover advantage isn't a moat by itself. It's a head start on building one. Six moats that still work Every one of these shares a trait: it builds up over time from real use. A clone that launches next year can copy the product on day one, but it starts this list at zero. 1. A graph that gets better with every user This was ChatGPT's answer for Chirpper, and it's the strongest one. The value isn't the code, it's the record of who invited who and which chains of people produce good stuff. A copycat gets the software and none of the history. For users to switch, they'd have to walk away from everything they built up. Test: Does your product get more useful for user #500 because users #1 through #499 showed up? 2. Connections to the systems your users depend on Anyone can build a personal finance or bookkeeping app in an afternoon now. The screens are the easy part. The hard part is getting the transaction data out of thousands of banks, reliably and cheaply. Intuit has spent decades on that. It signed direct data-sharing agreements with Chase and Wells Fargo back in 2017, so its apps pull bank data through APIs instead of scraping logins. That plumbing is a big part of why people keep paying for QuickBooks Online, which runs $38 to $85 a month on its two cheaper plans and up to $340 at the top. A new app has to rent that access, usually through an aggregator like Plaid. And renting is getting pricier: in September 2025, Plaid agreed to start paying JPMorgan Chase for customer data it used to get for free. Banks now charge the middlemen, and the middlemen charge you. Test: What outside systems does your product connect to that would take a competitor years, or a lot of money, to connect to? 3. Data you only get by operating Not data you scraped or bought, which anyone can get. Data that only exists because people use your thing: their history, their corrections, what worked and what didn't. Test: If a competitor copied your app today, what would be missing from their database that's in yours? 4. An audience you own If your users find you through a platform's algorithm, the platform owns your distribution and can turn it off. An email list, a community, or a site of your own is reach a clone can't copy. That's why I publish on my own site first and treat other platforms as places to repost. Bloggers used to know this. You owned your blog, your readers came to you, and nobody could throttle your reach. I think the modern version goes one step further: with AI, you can now build your own small social network the way people used to start a blog. I'll make that case in its own piece soon, because it deserves more than a paragraph. Test: If every social platform banned you tomorrow, how many people could you still reach? 5. Trust and a real person behind it AI can generate unlimited content and unlimited fake users. What it can't generate is first-hand experience or a verified human. Your track record, your name on the work, and proof that real people are behind it are getting more valuable, not less. Test: Would a reader or customer care if they found out it was you versus an anonymous clone? 6. Switching costs people actually feel Not fake lock-in, like making export hard. Real cost: the setup, the history, the habits, the reputation someone would have to rebuild somewhere else. Test: What does a user lose, concretely, if they leave you for a copy? Look at the list again and you'll see a common thread: connections. Connections between your users. Connections to the banks, carriers, or tools your users rely on. Connections to an audience. Connections to people who trust you. Code is a thing you can copy. A connection is a relationship, and relationships take time. Notice what's not on the list: speed, design, and being clever. Those help you win a race, but they don't protect a lead. The catch: a moat around an empty castle Here's what I wish I'd underlined that morning. ChatGPT said it in one line: the biggest risk isn't being copied, it's that the network never starts. Nobody clones a ghost town. Then we spent most of the session defending against problems that only show up with a crowd. Spam chains. Invite cartels gaming reputation. Whether replies should cost an invite so conversations stay high quality. ChatGPT treated that replies question as the decision that would make or break the network. I left replies wide open, with no login of any kind, for a long time. It didn't matter at all. Nobody was trying to reply. The noise never came, and neither did the commenters. Most of the moats above only start working once people show up. So the order matters: Get people in the door and give them a reason to stay. Make sure every one of them adds something a clone can't copy. Worry about defending it once there's something worth attacking. The best moat is one that starts filling on day one. Every invite on Chirpper adds to the graph from the very first user. That's the property to look for: a moat that grows as a side effect of normal use, not one you have to build later. Find your moat in 15 minutes Grab a notepad and answer these about your own project. Be honest, because nobody else is going to see it. The clone test. Imagine a competitor ships an exact copy of your product next month. Write down everything they'd still be missing. If the list is empty, you don't have a moat yet. The user #500 test. Does each new user make the product better for everyone else? If yes, that's your graph. Make it visible and make it grow. The plumbing test. List every outside system your product plugs into: banks, carriers, marketplaces, other people's software. Which of those connections would a new competitor have to beg, pay, or wait years for? Those are worth deepening. The database test. What do you collect that only exists because people use you? Start saving it now, even if you don't use it yet. The ban test. How many people can you reach without any platform's permission? If the answer is close to zero, start an email list or a home base this week. The name test. Would people care that it's you? If not, start putting your name and your real experience on the work. The day-one test. Which of your answers start working with your first user, and which need a crowd? Build the day-one ones first. Pick the one or two with the strongest answers. That's your moat. Spend your time making them deeper, and stop polishing the features a clone will copy anyway. Sources Chase and Intuit data-sharing agreement (Jan 2017) Wells Fargo and Intuit data exchange agreement (2017) Plaid agrees to pay JPMorgan for data access (Sept 2025) QuickBooks Online pricing, updated Oct 2026

title: Avoiding Email Delivery Issues
author: Kevinleary.net
summary: Google and Yahoo began enforcing bulk sender requirements in February 2024, and Microsoft followed on May 5, 2025, rejecting non-compliant bulk mail to Outlook, Hotmail and Live addresses with a permanent 550 5.7.515 error rather than quietly junking it. If your password resets, invoices or newsletters are landing in spam, the cause is almost always one of the layers below, and every one of them is fixable. This covers the full stack: DNS authentication with setup steps, the From/Reply-To mistakes that trip filters, compliance rules, domain and IP reputation, blocklist monitoring, and the testing tools that actually tell you where you stand. SPF, DKIM and DMARC Authentication These three DNS records are the price of admission now. Gmail and Yahoo require all three for anyone sending 5,000+ messages a day, Microsoft requires them for bulk senders, and even low-volume senders get scored on them. SPF: Who May Send for Your Domain SPF is a TXT record on your domain listing every server authorized to send mail claiming to be you. One record, every sender included: Type: TXT Host: @ Value: v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com include:sendgrid.net ip4:203.0.113.25 -all Setup steps: inventory every service that sends as your domain (Google Workspace, your ESP, your CRM, the web server sending form notifications), add each one’s include, then end with -all (hard fail) or ~all (soft fail). The two mistakes that break SPF: publishing more than one SPF record (the spec allows exactly one; merge them) and exceeding the 10 DNS lookup limit, which silently invalidates the whole record. Every include: costs lookups, so audit with a checker and drop services you no longer use, or use a flattening service if you genuinely need more than ten. DKIM: Cryptographic Proof the Message Wasn’t Altered DKIM signs each outgoing message with a private key; receivers verify it against a public key you publish in DNS under a selector: Type: TXT Host: s1._domainkey Value: v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIIBIjANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAAOCAQ8A... Setup steps: you don’t write this record by hand. Every legitimate sender (Google Workspace, SendGrid, Mailgun, Postmark, SES, your SMTP relay) generates the key pair and hands you the record or a CNAME to publish; you paste it in DNS and click verify. Use 2048-bit keys, publish a selector per sending service so one compromised key doesn’t take everything down, and rotate keys yearly. The common failure is a service left half-configured and signing with its own domain instead of yours, which brings us to alignment. DMARC: Policy for Failed Authentication DMARC tells receivers what to do when SPF or DKIM fail, and critically, it requires alignment : the domain in the From header your reader sees must match the domain that passed SPF or DKIM. Without DMARC, a spammer can pass SPF on their own domain while displaying yours in the From line. Type: TXT Host: _dmarc Value: v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@yourdomain.com; adkim=r; aspf=r Setup steps, in order: publish at p=none first, which enforces nothing but makes every major receiver email you aggregate reports showing exactly which services are sending as your domain and which are failing alignment. Read those reports for two to four weeks (a free parser like DMARC analyzers from EasyDMARC or Postmark’s DMARC digests makes them human-readable), fix every legitimate sender that’s failing, then tighten to p=quarantine and finally p=reject . Microsoft’s minimum is p=none , but none provides zero spoofing protection and does nothing for your reputation; reject is the destination. Once you’re at enforcement, BIMI lets you publish your logo next to messages in Gmail and Yahoo, which is cosmetic but signals exactly the kind of sender filters trust. From, Reply-To and Formatting Mistakes Authentication gets you to the door; the message itself still has to not look like spam. From domain mismatch – Sending “from” yourdomain.com through an ESP that signs as esp-mail.com fails DMARC alignment. Always complete the custom domain authentication step in your ESP. Reply-To pointing somewhere unrelated – A From at yourdomain.com with a Reply-To at a random Gmail address is a classic phishing pattern. Keep Reply-To on the same domain, or at minimum a recognizably related one, and make it a real monitored mailbox. noreply@ addresses – Filters increasingly score on engagement, and an address that invites zero replies earns zero positive engagement. Replies are the strongest positive signal a mailbox provider sees; accept them. HTML with no plain-text part – Multipart messages with a real text/plain alternative score better than HTML-only. Most ESPs generate it; broken custom senders often skip it. Link text that doesn’t match the href – Displaying one URL while linking another is the single most phishing-correlated content pattern. Related: raw link shorteners (bit.ly) in email bodies, which spammers burned long ago. Image-heavy, text-light bodies – One big image with ten words of text is spammer camouflage. Keep a sensible text-to-image ratio. Sloppy HTML – Unclosed tags, pasted-from-Word markup, and $0 font tricks all correlate with junk. Templates from any mainstream ESP are fine; hand-rolled HTML deserves a lint. Tracking domains that aren’t yours – Open and click tracking rewrites links through your ESP’s shared tracking domain, whose reputation you share with every other customer. Set up a custom tracking CNAME (track.yourdomain.com) so clicks resolve through your own name. Compliance: Unsubscribe and the Law This is both a legal requirement and a filtering input, because providers measure how you handle people who want out. One-click unsubscribe headers (RFC 8058) – Gmail, Yahoo and Microsoft all require bulk mail to carry List-Unsubscribe and List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click headers, and to honor them within two days. This is the header-level unsubscribe button in Gmail’s UI, separate from the link in your footer. Any real ESP adds it; verify yours does. CAN-SPAM (US) – Working unsubscribe honored within 10 business days, a valid physical postal address in every commercial message, and no deceptive subject lines or headers. Penalties are per message. GDPR (EU) and CASL (Canada) – Consent-based rather than opt-out-based: you need provable opt-in before sending marketing at all. CASL fines are severe. Spam-rate ceiling – Gmail’s enforced threshold is a 0.3% user-reported spam rate, with under 0.1% as the stated target. Making unsubscribe hard doesn’t retain subscribers; it converts them into spam complaints that poison delivery to everyone else on your list. Sending Domain Authority and Content Relevance Mailbox providers keep a reputation score on your domain the same way Google keeps one for search, and it’s built on history: how long the domain has sent mail, how consistently, and how recipients react. Never send cold from a fresh domain. A domain registered last week blasting 10,000 messages is the textbook spam signature. Age the domain, send low volumes to engaged recipients first, and ramp over weeks (warmup). Use subdomains to isolate reputation. The standard architecture is transactional mail from one subdomain (mail.yourdomain.com), marketing from another (news.yourdomain.com), corporate one-to-one from the root. A newsletter mistake then can’t drag your receipts into spam. Send from a domain with real, related content. Filters and the humans reviewing mitigation requests both check whether the sending domain resolves to a live site whose content matches the mail. A newsletter about WordPress sent from a domain hosting a WordPress consultancy is coherent; mail from a bare parked domain, or content mismatched with the site, reads as a snowshoe spam setup. Keep the root domain’s site alive, relevant and linked from your messages. Keep volume consistent. Reputation systems model your normal. Sending nothing for two months and then a 50,000-message burst looks like a compromised account even when it’s just your holiday campaign; ramp into spikes. Sending IP Reputation Below the domain sits the IP, and the right answer depends on volume. Under roughly 100K messages/month: use your ESP’s shared pools. A good provider polices its pools, and a shared IP with constant healthy traffic beats a dedicated IP you can’t keep warm. High volume: dedicated IP, warmed properly. Two to six weeks of gradually increasing sends to your most engaged recipients before full volume, and never let it go cold. Never send bulk from your web server’s IP. Your WordPress box has no sending reputation, shares a neighborhood with whoever your host put next to you, and PHP mail() from it is the fastest route to the junk folder. Route everything through authenticated SMTP or an API-based provider; I covered the small-scale version of this in my Google SMTP post. Checking Blocklists and Monitoring Reputation Do this on a schedule, not after the complaints start: Blocklist sweep – MXToolbox’s blacklist check runs your domain and IP against 100+ lists in one shot. The ones that matter: Spamhaus (SBL/XBL/DBL), Barracuda, SpamCop, SURBL. Most lists have self-service delisting once you’ve fixed the cause; Spamhaus listings mean a real problem to resolve first. Google Postmaster Tools – Free, and the only first-party view of how Gmail scores you: domain and IP reputation tiers, spam-rate trend, authentication success rates. Mandatory for anyone sending volume to Gmail. Microsoft SNDS and JMRP – The Outlook equivalents: SNDS shows your IP’s traffic and complaint view, JMRP feeds you the actual complaints so you can suppress those recipients. DMARC aggregate reports – Your ongoing radar for both spoofing attempts and legitimate services drifting out of alignment. Testing Deliverability Two tools cover 95% of needs: Mail-Tester (free) for the quick check. Send one message to the address it generates and get a 10-point score with every deduction itemized: SPF/DKIM/DMARC results, blocklist hits, content flags, broken headers. It’s the right first stop every time you change DNS, templates or providers. Don’t chase 10/10 religiously; chase the specific deductions. GlockApps for real inbox placement. My recommendation when it matters: it sends your actual campaign to a seed list of ~70 real mailboxes across Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo and others and shows you where it landed (inbox, promotions, spam, missing) per provider, plus blocklist and DMARC monitoring. Plans run $59 to $129 a month, and one month of it diagnosing a placement problem pays for itself. The honest caveat with any seed test: seed inboxes have no engagement history with you, so results approximate real-world placement rather than guarantee it, which is why Postmaster Tools stays in the loop as ground truth. For DNS-layer verification specifically, learndmarc.com visualizes a live SPF/DKIM/DMARC evaluation of a real message, and EasyDMARC or dmarcian make the ongoing report monitoring painless. Common Patterns That Get Flagged The shortlist of behaviors that reliably trigger filters, independent of everything above: Purchased or scraped lists, which are salted with spam traps: addresses that never opted into anything and exist purely to catch you. One trap hit craters a reputation. No list hygiene: hard bounces left on the list signal scraping, and Microsoft’s 2025 rules explicitly require bounce management. Suppress hard bounces immediately and prune recipients who haven’t engaged in 6-12 months. Sudden volume spikes from a quiet domain or IP. Mismatched or deceptive subject lines (“Re:” on a first contact, fake forward prefixes). Sending everything to everyone instead of segmenting by engagement; low open rates across a whole list drag the domain down for your best recipients too. Rotating domains or IPs to outrun a bad reputation, which is literally the definition of snowshoe spam and is pattern-matched aggressively. Setup Order If you’re starting from spam-folder purgatory, fix things in this sequence: authenticate (SPF, DKIM, DMARC at p=none), read a Mail-Tester result and clear every deduction, fix alignment and move DMARC to reject over a month, add the one-click unsubscribe headers, set up Postmaster Tools and SNDS, sweep blocklists and delist, then run a GlockApps placement test to confirm. Deliverability is not one setting; it’s the accumulation of a sender that authenticates cleanly, mails people who asked for it, and makes leaving painless. Mailbox providers measure all three, and they’re measuring whether you’re worth delivering.

title: There Is No MP3 on YouTube: Why I Label the Audio Button M4A
author: Mobeen Ahmed
summary: When I first wired YouTube support into my downloader, the audio button said "MP3". Everybody expects an MP3 button. Every downloader site has one. So I added one without thinking. Then I looked at what was actually coming back from the provider API. What YouTube actually serves YouTube does not ship MP3 files. The audio tracks inside YouTube's streams are M4A (AAC) or Opus in a WebM container. That is what the site itself streams to your browser. An MP3 file only exists if somebody decodes that audio and re-encodes it into MP3 — a conversion step with its own CPU cost, its own quality loss, and on shared hosting, a whole dependency chain (ffmpeg) I do not have and cannot install. So the honest options are: Serve the audio exactly as YouTube provides it — M4A or Opus. Transcode to MP3 on the server — slow, lossy, and fragile on cheap hosting. I chose option one. Why transcoding on the fly is a bad deal on shared hosting My site runs on plain shared hosting: PHP, no shell ffmpeg, no background workers, no Redis. Transcoding means spawning an ffmpeg process per request, holding a connection open while it works, and praying the host's process killer does not notice. One busy afternoon and the whole site crawls — or the host suspends the account. Even if the plumbing were free, transcoding is lossy-to-lossy. YouTube's AAC at 128 kbps converted to MP3 at 128 kbps loses detail twice for zero benefit. The visitor gets a worse file, slower. What the button says now The audio button on ramrom.io says "Audio (M4A)". The homepage copy that used to promise MP3 now says M4A. It felt like a downgrade the day I made the change — MP3 is the word people search for — but the file a visitor receives is exactly what YouTube's own servers produced, and it plays everywhere: phones, browsers, car stereos. Nobody has complained. A couple of people noticed and said the download was fast, which is the part I actually care about. The wider lesson This is a small thing, but it is the same instinct behind every honest decision on the site: label what is actually there. A "4K MP4 with sound" button that hands you a 360p file with sound is the same lie as an "MP3" button that hands you M4A — it just sounds better in the marketing copy. I would rather ship a button that says something unfashionable and delivers exactly that. If you are building a downloader, check what your provider actually returns for the audio-only formats. If it is M4A or Opus, label it that way. Your users' devices already play it, and you get to skip the entire transcoding headache on day one.

title: WooCommerce, Shopify or Custom eCommerce?
author: Kevinleary.net
summary: Each eCommerce system in this comparison can be the best option, but there is no universal “best one,” only the one that is best for you, your situation, and your business. I build and support stores on all three of these approaches for clients, so this is not a feature checklist copied from marketing pages. It is my honest opinion on when Shopify, WooCommerce, or a fully custom eCommerce build is the right call, where each one shines, and where each one quietly costs you more than you expected. The Cheat Sheet Platform Ideal For Watch Out For Cost Reality Shopify Established brands moving online, small businesses selling straightforward products, and anyone who wants a store that just works with almost no maintenance Transaction fees, limited control over checkout and URL structure, weaker content and SEO flexibility Predictable monthly fee that looks more expensive than it is; almost everything operational is included WooCommerce Businesses that win on organic search and need heavily optimized product landing pages, or complex configurable products like decking and fencing Plugin-stack builds, premium add-on subscriptions, hosting and caching problems, and providers who assemble instead of engineer Cheaper on paper, more expensive in practice; hosting, maintenance, and plugin fees add up in the short run, not just the long run Custom eCommerce SaaS and subscription business models, custom products and product workflows, and businesses where the buying experience is the differentiator Choosing the wrong builder; AI-generated code without engineering experience behind it creates the same mess it was supposed to avoid Higher initial investment, dramatically lower long-term cost for a serious business, and AI code generation has cut the entry price significantly Shopify: For a Hosted Store That Needs Little Maintenance If you have an established, well-recognized brand and you want to start selling online, or you are a small business owner who wants very easy, very automated maintenance of your shop, and what you sell is relatively straightforward, Shopify is always the best option. That is my opinion, and I say it as someone who makes a living building the alternatives. Some people hem and haw over the fact that Shopify can look slightly more expensive than a hosted WordPress site running WooCommerce. In my experience, WooCommerce and WordPress will always cost you more, and not just in the long run, in the short run too. Behind the scenes, Shopify takes care of an enormous amount for you: hosting, security, PCI compliance, checkout optimization, software updates, and uptime during traffic spikes. That is well worth what it charges. A few things you get with Shopify that are easy to take for granted: Scaling is not your problem. You never worry about your store falling over during a rush of sales, a holiday promotion, or a viral moment. That capacity is baked into the platform. Fulfillment integrations are reliable. You can connect directly to fulfillment providers in far more dependable ways than the equivalent WordPress plugin stack. The checkout converts. Shopify has spent years optimizing one checkout flow across millions of stores, including Shop Pay. You benefit from all of it on day one. Maintenance is nearly zero. There are no plugin updates to test, no PHP versions to manage, and no security patches to schedule. The trade-offs are real but narrow: you pay transaction fees, you accept Shopify’s URL structure and checkout constraints, and deep content or SEO customization is harder than it is on WordPress. For most product businesses, none of that outweighs a system that simply does not break. WooCommerce: When Search Rankings or Product Complexity Drive the Business WooCommerce is not often my recommendation, but it has genuine advantages in two situations. The first is search. If your growth depends on organic visibility, WooCommerce gives you the ability to create heavily optimized product landing pages for SEO and AI search that can outrank what Shopify allows. You control the markup, the structured data, the internal linking, the page speed work, and the content around every product. Shopify keeps a lot of that surface area locked down; WordPress hands you all of it. The second is advanced product configuration. Businesses selling things like decking, fencing, or anything built from measurements and options often need configurators that go beyond a dropdown and a price. This kind of thing is possible in Shopify, but it is difficult, and you regularly hit the limits of what the platform will let you do. On WooCommerce you can build exactly the configuration flow the product requires. Here is the part most comparisons leave out: a good WooCommerce developer changes the effectiveness of this platform dramatically, and the wrong one is how WooCommerce earned its reputation for being slow and fragile. The thing to watch out for is any provider whose plan is to piece together a pile of plugins to build your shop, especially premium plugins with recurring fees. Every plugin is code you did not write, running on every page load, with its own update cycle and its own conflicts. With code generation through Claude and OpenAI’s models, many of those solutions can now be built cleanly and minimally in custom code. A small, purpose-built feature should replace a premium subscription add-on, not sit alongside six of them. If a proposal for your store reads like a shopping list of paid plugins, keep looking. And budget honestly. WooCommerce’s software is free, but quality hosting, caching that actually handles cart sessions , security, updates, and ongoing development are not. That is why the “cheaper than Shopify” argument usually collapses within the first year. Custom eCommerce: For SaaS, Subscriptions and Product Workflows Custom eCommerce is the ideal choice for anyone building a software-as-a-service or subscription-based business model around a custom product or product workflow. If the way people buy, configure, onboard, or use your product is itself the differentiator, no off-the-shelf platform is going to express it well. A lot of people balk at this option because they assume the initial cost is high and the lifetime cost is higher. For a serious business, it is the opposite: provided you find a reasonable provider, the initial investment is far outweighed by what you save later. I have seen subscription systems bolted together with WooCommerce, and it always pains me to see how much time, effort, and money went into forcing plugins to approximate what the business actually needed. The result is a patchwork that behaves like a house of cards: every plugin update is a risk, every new feature is a workaround stacked on a workaround, and nobody can safely touch it. With a custom system you build precisely what you want, which is far more maintainable and sustainable long term: No growth ceiling. When the business scales up, you are not fighting platform limits or plugin performance; the architecture was designed for your model from the start. The ideal user experience. You can create exactly the buying and onboarding flow that works best for your specific audience, not the closest approximation a theme allows. Real ownership. The system is an asset you control, not a stack of rented subscriptions that can change pricing or disappear. If you want to set yourself apart and you have a highly specific idea of what will work best for your audience, this is the road to take. The good news is that AI code generation has drastically reduced the barrier to entry; you no longer need to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars to create a real web application. I wrote more about that shift in replacing SaaS with custom software . That said, you still need a solid custom eCommerce provider , or at minimum someone who genuinely knows how to architect, scale, and maintain a web application. Throwing prompts at an AI without that background is dangerous, and it produces the same fragile mess as the worst WooCommerce builds, just faster. Which One Should You Choose? Strip away the feature charts and the decision is simpler than the industry makes it: Choose Shopify if your products are straightforward and you want a store that runs itself. Pay the fee, skip the headaches, and spend your energy on the brand. Choose WooCommerce if organic search is your growth engine or your products need real configuration logic, and only with a developer who writes lean custom code instead of stacking premium plugins. Choose custom if you are building a SaaS or subscription business, or the buying experience itself is your competitive edge. The upfront cost buys you a system that fits, scales, and belongs to you. There is no wrong platform here, only a wrong match. Pick the one that fits how your business actually makes money, and be just as careful about who builds it as what it is built on.

title: Learn React Free
author: Khawaja Khurram (MAK)
summary: 📚 This article was originally published on MAK Studio . Check out the full interactive lesson with live demos and code examples. Home › Courses › React ⚛️ Learning Path · 2026 Learn React. The most-used frontend library. React is how modern web apps are built. Every major company — Meta, Netflix, Airbnb, Uber, Shopify — uses it. Components, state, hooks, and the mental model that makes UIs predictable. This track teaches all of it, with real code and working examples. Every lesson assumes you already know JavaScript — if you don't, complete that track first. ~6 weeks, 1 hr/day Intermediate React 19 · modern The Path 5 Concepts Live demo Mistakes Projects FAQ Prerequisite: JavaScript. React is JavaScript. If you don't understand functions, arrays, objects, arrow functions, closures, and the DOM, learning React becomes memorization. Spend 2-3 months on the JavaScript track first. Every React tutorial assumes this foundation, and skipping it is the #1 reason beginners give up. What you'll learn: components, JSX, props, state, hooks (useState, useEffect, useRef, useContext), routing, forms, and the mental model that makes React apps predictable. Every example has working code you can preview. Why React Every interactive website needs to update its UI when data changes. In vanilla JavaScript, you manipulate the DOM manually — querySelector, createElement, appendChild. As apps grow, this becomes unwieldy. React's insight was that the UI should be a function of state: when state changes, React computes what changed and updates only what's necessary. No more manual DOM tracking. That's why it won. React didn't win because it's fast (Vue and Svelte are faster). It won because it made large apps tractable. When your app has 100 components, 20 shared states, and 50 user interactions, React's mental model — state flows down, events flow up — is what makes the codebase possible to reason about. The syntax is learnable in a week; the mental model is what you spend months mastering. The payoff is real. React is the most-in-demand frontend skill in job listings. It's the foundation of React Native (mobile apps), Next.js (full-stack apps), and Remix. Learning React isn't just learning a library — it's learning the way modern frontend works. 🗺️ The 6-week path Follow these in order. Each phase builds on the one before it. 1 Setup & first component Week 1 · ~3 hours Install Vite, create a project, write your first component. Understand JSX — how HTML-like syntax compiles to JavaScript. See how React renders a component to the DOM. This is the entire setup — modern tooling makes it 3 commands. ViteJSXComponentsRender → Your first component 2 Props & composition Week 2 · ~4 hours Props pass data from parent to child. Children compose — a component can contain other components. This is how you build UIs: small pieces, combined into bigger pieces. The mental model: data flows down, functions flow up (as callbacks). PropsChildrenCompositionProp types → Props & composition 3 State with useState Week 3 · ~5 hours State is data that changes over time. useState gives function components local state. When state changes, React re-renders. This is the core of React — understanding when and why re-renders happen is the skill. useStateRe-rendersBatchingLifting state → State & useState 4 Events & forms Week 4 · ~4 hours React events look like HTML but work like JavaScript. Forms need controlled inputs — state that mirrors input value. Submit handlers, validation, and the difference between controlled and uncontrolled inputs. This is where most real apps spend their complexity. onClickonChangeControlled inputsForm submit → Events & forms 5 useEffect & side effects Week 4-5 · ~5 hours useEffect runs code after render — data fetching, subscriptions, timers. The dependency array controls when it runs. This is the hook most beginners misuse, so we'll make it clear. Once you understand useEffect, you understand most of React. useEffectDependenciesCleanupData fetching → useEffect 6 Lists & keys Week 5 · ~3 hours Rendering arrays of items is the most common React pattern. Keys tell React which item is which when the list changes. Getting keys right is the difference between smooth updates and mysterious bugs. .map()KeysFilteringSorting → Lists & keys 7 Build something Week 6 · ~6 hours Pick a project from the list below. Build it. Break it. Rebuild it. The project is where the mental model clicks — everything before this is preparation. Two weeks of building will teach you more than two months of tutorials. PlanBuildDebugShip → Project list 🎯 The 5 concepts that matter most If you only truly understand five things about React, make it these. 1. UI is a function of state You don't tell React what to change — you tell it what state is, and it figures out the DOM updates. This is declarative vs imperative. Once you stop trying to "update the DOM" and start "changing state," React becomes simple. 2. Props flow down, events flow up Parent passes data to child via props. Child communicates back by calling functions the parent passed down. That's the entire data flow. No two-way binding, no global state in the component tree. 3. State lives at the closest common ancestor If two components need the same state, put it in their nearest common parent. Pass it down via props. This is "lifting state up" — and it's the standard pattern for shared state. 4. Every render is a snapshot When React re-renders, it's not "updating" — it's calling your component function again with current state and comparing the result. Understanding this makes effects, closures, and stale state make sense. 5. Effects are for external sync useEffect runs after render to sync with things outside React — APIs, subscriptions, the DOM. If you're updating state in useEffect, you probably want a derived value or event handler instead. 🎬 See it in action The classic counter — the simplest React component. State, event, render. Counter.jsx import { useState } from ' react ' ; function Counter () { const [ count , setCount ] = useState ( 0 ); return ( # { count } setCount ( count - 1 )} style = {{ padding : ' 0.5rem 1rem ' , marginRight : ' 0.5rem ' }} > − 1 setCount ( count + 1 )} style = {{ padding : ' 0.5rem 1rem ' }} > + 1 ); } export default Counter ; Three things are happening in this component. (1) useState(0) creates a state variable count initialized to 0. (2) The render function uses count to display the value. (3) The buttons call setCount to change state, which triggers a re-render. That's React: state, render, update. Every component you'll ever write follows this pattern. ⚠️ Common mistakes (from real beginners) Each of these will cost you hours if you don't know it. Learning React before JavaScript The #1 reason beginners fail. If you don't understand arrow functions, destructuring, map/filter, and closures, every React tutorial becomes memorization. Complete the JavaScript track first. Mutating state directly items.push(x) or user.name = 'Bob' doesn't trigger re-renders — React compares state by reference. Fix: use setters that return new values: setItems([...items, x]) . Forgetting keys in lists Rendering an array without keys produces console warnings and buggy updates. Fix: {items.map(item => )} . Use stable IDs, not array indices. Using array indices as keys If items reorder, delete, or insert, index keys cause wrong components to keep wrong state. Fix: use a stable unique ID from your data. Generate one with crypto.randomUUID() if needed. useEffect dependency mistakes Missing dependencies cause stale closures. Extra dependencies cause infinite loops. Fix: install the eslint-plugin-react-hooks plugin — it catches both automatically. useEffect for derived state If you compute values in useEffect and store them in state, you have a bug waiting to happen. Fix: compute derived values in the render function directly. useEffect is for external sync, not for computing. Prop drilling 5 levels deep Passing props through 5 components that don't use them is a smell. Fix: use Context or component composition (pass children, not props). Calling hooks conditionally if (x) { useState(...) } breaks React — hooks must be called in the same order every render. Fix: call hooks at the top of the component, unconditionally. 🔨 Projects by difficulty Build these in order. Each one uses only concepts from the phases before it. Beginner Counter Increment, decrement, reset. Uses useState + events. The hello world of React. Beginner To-do list Add, complete, delete items. Uses state + lists + keys. The classic first real project. Beginner Color picker Pick a color, see it applied. Uses controlled inputs + state. First form. Intermediate Weather app Fetch from an API, show current weather. Uses useEffect + async/await + loading states. First data-fetching app. Intermediate Movie search Search box with debouncing, results grid, loading + error states. Uses everything so far. Looks like a real app. Advanced Full blog Multi-page with routing, forms, CRUD against localStorage. Uses React Router + forms + all hooks. Ship-ready. ❓ Frequently asked questions Do I need to know JavaScript before React? Yes — absolutely. React is a JavaScript library. If you don't understand functions, arrays, objects, arrow functions, and closures, learning React becomes memorization instead of understanding. Spend 2-3 months on JavaScript first. Complete the JavaScript track on this site, then come back to React. What is React? React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. Instead of manipulating the DOM directly, you describe what the UI should look like as a function of state, and React updates the DOM efficiently when state changes. What is JSX? JSX is a syntax extension that lets you write HTML-like code inside JavaScript. Instead of createElement('div', ...), you write ... . JSX is not valid JavaScript — it's compiled by a build tool (Babel, Vite) into React.createElement calls. What is the difference between props and state? Props are data passed from a parent component to a child — they're read-only. State is data that a component owns and can change over time. When state changes, the component re-renders. The mental model: props flow down, state lives inside a component. What is a hook in React? A hook is a function that lets a component 'hook into' React features. useState adds state to a function component. useEffect runs side effects after render. useContext reads context. useRef holds a mutable value across renders. Hooks were introduced in React 16.8 (2019) and replaced class components as the standard way to write React. What is the difference between a class component and a function component? Function components are the modern standard. They're just JavaScript functions that return JSX. Class components use ES6 classes and lifecycle methods. Function components with hooks are shorter, easier to test, and align with functional programming. Do I need a build tool to use React? Not strictly. You can use React via CDN with Babel in the browser. But for real projects, use Vite (the modern standard) or Next.js (for server-rendered apps). Vite is the easiest starting point — three commands and you're running. What should I build after this course? A to-do list (learn state + events), a weather app (learn API fetching + loading states), a movie search (learn debouncing + rendering lists), a full blog (learn routing + forms), a dashboard (learn complex state + layouts). Each project teaches a specific skill.
