title: Corporate PowerPoint decks with AI, for free: slides as code, QA as the gate
author: sebyx07
summary: Ask an AI chat to "make me a board deck" and you usually get one of three things: A wall of Markdown you still have to paste into PowerPoint. A picture of slides that nobody can edit. A .pptx where the text spills off slide 4, the chart is a screenshot, and the closing slide says "Thank you! Questions?" I wanted a fourth option: the AI writes the deck, a machine proves it is correct, and a second AI with fresh eyes judges it. That project is PowerPoint Factory . It is MIT-licensed and you can clone it today. The sample: a 20-slide Q4 board review for Halden Logistics, a fictional company. Every shape, chart and table is native and editable in PowerPoint. What "free" means here The factory is free. MIT license, no SaaS seat, no per-deck fee, no watermark. The toolchain is free. Bun , LibreOffice (headless rendering), poppler and open metric-compatible fonts (Carlito, Caladea, Liberation, Gelasio). AI images are optional. Generated photos, video and music come from Kubeez and cost credits. Without a key you get labeled placeholders and everything else still builds. Results are cached and committed, so you never pay twice for the same image. You bring the agent. It is built for Claude Code, and any agent that reads AGENTS.md can drive it. You can also write the recipes by hand: they are just TypeScript. A slide is data, not coordinates Every slide is a small typed recipe, one file per slide. You pick a layout by the message you want to land, not by where boxes go: // slides/06-margin-bridge.ts import { slide } from " @/slide " ; export default slide ({ layout : " waterfall " , eyebrow : " Results " , title : " Pricing and routes added $19M of operating profit; wage inflation took back $6M " , steps : [ { label : " Q4 2025 " , value : 46 , total : true }, { label : " Pricing " , value : 9 }, { label : " Route consolidation " , value : 6 }, { label : " Wage inflation " , value : - 6 }, { label : " Q4 2026 " , value : 55 , total : true }, ], prefix : " $ " , suffix : " M " , source : " Halden finance; operating profit, $M " , notes : " The operational levers more than offset wage inflation. " , }); That becomes this. Real shapes, not an image: This is why AI is good at it. An LLM is bad at pixel geometry and good at structured data. Layouts handle the geometry, so the model only has to get the content and the story right. There are 23 built-in layouts: cover, agenda, summary, stats, chart, waterfall, table (with RAG status and Harvey balls), 2×2 matrix, process, timeline, roadmap, next steps, references and more. Charts (column, bar, stacked, line, area, pie, doughnut) are native PowerPoint charts, so finance can still click in and fix a number. Native table with highlight and total rows Gantt roadmap with a "today" line The part that makes it corporate-grade: QA Generating a .pptx is easy. Generating one you would send to a board is not. So every build runs about 40 checks, and each one comes with a → fix hint the agent can act on: Layout: text overflow, measured with metric-twin fonts so wrapping matches PowerPoint; overlaps; safe margins; minimum font sizes; titles kept to two lines or fewer. Accessibility: WCAG AA contrast against the real backdrop, including photos and translucent scrims; alt text; real title placeholders so outline view and screen readers work. Copy discipline: at most 6 bullets and about 70 words per slide, no placeholder text, no emoji, and a list of banned slop words ("leverage synergies", I'm looking at you). Story and charts: action titles, a source line on data slides, no pies with negative values, axes that start at zero, and no "Thank you" closer. The deck ends on decisions. Rendered pixels: LibreOffice renders every slide to PDF and PNG, then checks for blank slides, ink touching the edge, and a pixel diff against an approved baseline. The output folder gives you, and the agent, everything needed to look at the result: a contact sheet, one PNG per slide, a QA report, and an outline containing only the titles. If the titles alone don't tell the story, the deck isn't done. The loop git clone https://github.com/sebyx07/power-point-factory && cd power-point-factory bin/setup # bun install, .env, checks LibreOffice + poppler + fonts bin/deck loop # build + QA + screenshots of the sample deck bin/deck new acme q1-review board-update --theme ledger claude # then: /deck acme "Q1 board review — revenue 2M, +11%…" The /deck command follows the same workflow a consultant would: Ghost deck. Write the action titles first. Each is one sentence with the takeaway, 15 words or fewer. Recipe. One file per slide, with the layout chosen by the message. bin/deck loop . Fix every ✖ until QA passes. Look. The agent reads the contact sheet and the full-size screenshots. Fresh eyes. A separate deck-reviewer agent, which never saw the recipe, judges the screenshots and returns ship , fix or rebuild . Export. bin/deck export is QA-gated and writes Company - Title - date.pptx/.pdf . The agent is also told never to invent facts. A missing number becomes a TBD in the speaker notes and is listed back to you. It never ends up on a slide, and QA fails if one does. Real photography without a stock-photo subscription: Kubeez Stock photos are where a lot of corporate decks die: the same handshake, the same glass tower, and a license nobody checked. The factory gets its imagery from Kubeez instead, and it's what makes the sample deck look like an agency made it: Every photo in the Halden deck is a Kubeez generation, including the cover and the warehouse shots. Why it fits a slides-as-code workflow so well: One API for every kind of media. Images (text-to-image and image-to-image), video (text-to-video and image-to-video), music beds and background removal, so you can make transparent cut-outs of products or people. You can pick the model per job and choose resolutions up to 4K on models that support it. Slide-shaped output. Request 16:9 for full-bleed slides, 3:4 for a half-slide cover, 1:1 for objects or 21:9 for banners. No cropping. The agent can use it directly. There's a REST API for builds and an MCP server ( mcp.kubeez.com ) so Claude Code can generate and preview media in the conversation. Built for caching. The factory hashes each prompt spec and stores the result in the deck's assets/generated/ folder, which you commit. Rebuilds are offline and free, and teammates who clone the repo never pay again for the same image. bin/kubeez generate "aerial photo of a logistics hub at dawn, 35mm, natural light" --aspect 16:9 bin/kubeez remove-bg ./assets/product.png bin/kubeez balance In a recipe, an image is just a prop. The factory generates it on the first build and reads it from the cache after that. Add KUBEEZ_API_KEY to .env and you're set. Brand once, reuse forever Each company gets a "brand brain": BRAND.md for voice, logo rules, colors and approved facts, brand.ts for theme tokens, plus logos and reusable photos. Four built-in themes (cobalt, ledger, graphite, terracotta) all pass a WCAG AA test, and extendTheme puts your colors on top. A brand-reviewer agent checks claims and logo use against BRAND.md before anything ships. Motion without the effect soup Pick one motion profile per deck: none (for read-ahead decks), subtle (the default, a fade transition), build (click reveals) or keynote (Morph). Per-slide effect soup isn't an option. Try it Repo: https://github.com/sebyx07/power-point-factory Want to see the result without installing anything? The sample .pptx and PDF are committed. AI images, video and music: https://kubeez.com . Get an API key at https://kubeez.com/settings/api-keys . Issues and PRs are welcome. The repo is maintained by an AI agent that triages, reviews and merges on green CI. If you build a deck with it, I'd like to see the contact sheet. Drop it in the comments.

Granular RBAC Scopes: Restrict access to specific capabilities ( subdomains:read , subdomains:write , dns:write , webhooks:read ). Subdomain Sandboxing ( allowed_subdomains ): Restrict an agent's token to only manage domains matching a specific prefix (e.g. pr-* or dev-preview ). title: Google’s August 2026 Spam Update
author: Kevinleary.net
summary: The update began August 18, 2026 and completed in roughly 2 days and 16 hours according to Google’s ranking updates dashboard , the second spam update of the year after June’s and the third counting March’s. That rollout speed matters on its own: spam updates used to take a week or more, and a sub-three-day cycle means Google’s spam systems are classifying at a pace where there is no window to notice a drop and react mid-rollout. You find out after it’s done. What a Spam Update Is Spam updates are improvements to Google’s automated spam detection, the systems behind what Google calls SpamBrain, and they enforce the published spam policies rather than general quality ranking. That distinction matters for diagnosis: a core update rebalances what good content ranks; a spam update removes or demotes content Google has classified as violating policy. There’s no manual action notice in Search Console, no email, and nothing to appeal. Google’s own guidance for affected sites is blunt: review the spam policies, fix what violates them, and expect recovery to take months as the systems revalidate the site, often not fully until a following update. Which Sites Were Affected The spam policies most relevant to legitimate businesses in 2026 are three: Scaled content abuse. Publishing large volumes of pages that exist to capture search queries rather than help anyone, and Google is explicit that this applies whether the pages were made by AI, humans, or both. The AI angle is what changed the game: tools that generate 500 “answers” a week turned every business into a potential content farm, and this is the policy that catches them. Doorway-style templated pages. Fleets of near-identical pages, one per city, per keyword, per tool, per industry, where only the noun changes. Programmatic SEO built this way was already living on borrowed time. Site reputation abuse. Third-party content riding on a strong domain’s authority, the “parasite SEO” pattern Google has been dismantling since 2024. Who feels it most: sites that scaled page count as a strategy. Local service businesses with 200 thin city pages, SaaS companies with auto-generated comparison and glossary fleets, publishers running AI content pipelines with light editing, and affiliates stacking templated reviews. Who generally doesn’t: sites with fewer pages that each carry real expertise, evidence, and a reason to exist. Why Consolidating Content Helps For years my core recommendation for both SEO and AI answer engines has been consolidation: fewer, denser, more authoritative pages instead of a thin page per keyword variant. Merge the overlapping posts, 301 the losers into the winner, kill the pages that exist only to exist, and make every surviving URL the best available answer to the question it targets. It’s how I’ve approached AEO work long before this update, and the August rollout is Google formally agreeing. The logic was never mysterious. Authority signals concentrated on one strong page outrank the same signals split across five weak ones, AI assistants citing sources pick the page that answers completely rather than the fragment farm, and every thin page on a domain drags down the classifier’s read of everything else. Scaled content dilutes; consolidation compounds. What changed in August is the penalty side of the ledger: the thin half of your site is no longer just dead weight, it’s a policy liability attached to your domain. I practice this on my own site, not just client work: overlapping articles get merged and redirected into one canonical piece, templated landing pages get individually written titles, descriptions, and genuinely distinct content or they get removed, and pages with no search or citation value get pruned. The result is a site where every URL can survive a spam classifier looking for scaled patterns, because none of it is scaled. If Your Traffic Dropped: Diagnose First Confirm the timing. In Search Console, compare the days before August 18 against August 21 onward. A drop that starts inside that window and holds is this update; a drift that started earlier is something else, and plenty of August drops are actually the ongoing wobble from May’s core update. Identify what dropped. Segment by page, not just query. Spam updates typically crater a class of pages, the templated fleet, the AI-generated section, the guest-post directory, while the rest of the site holds. The pattern of what fell is the diagnosis. Audit against the policies, honestly. Read the scaled content and doorway definitions and ask the uncomfortable question: would a human visiting these pages agree each one deserves to exist on its own? If the answer requires explaining your content strategy, the classifier already answered it. Consolidating Pages to Recover Recovery from a spam classification does not come from retouching titles on 400 thin pages. The playbook that works: Merge overlapping content. Take each cluster of pages chasing variants of one topic, combine the genuinely useful material into a single strong page, and 301 the rest into it. Redirects preserve the link equity; deletion without redirects throws it away. De-template what remains. If a set of pages must exist as a set, landing pages per integration or per service area, every one needs unique titles, descriptions, and substantive content that could not be swapped to a different page by changing one word. Real examples, real data, real differences. Prune without mercy. Pages with no traffic, no links, no conversions, and no distinct answer should be removed or noindexed. Shrinking a site is often the single fastest quality signal you can send. Slow the pipeline. If AI is part of your content production, and it reasonably can be, the output needs editorial judgment, first-hand evidence, and a publishing rate tied to what you can actually verify, not what the tool can generate. Then wait, actively. Google is explicit that spam recovery takes months and often lands with a later update. Keep publishing consolidated, genuinely useful work in the meantime, because the reassessment judges what it finds then, not your remediation memo. The uncomfortable summary for businesses: Google spent two and a half days in August enforcing what quality-focused practitioners have said for years, that page count is not a strategy. If your site got hit, the path back is making it smaller and better. If it didn’t, the update is your argument for never letting anyone scale it thin in the first place. Either way, consolidation stopped being a philosophy in August; it’s now the compliance posture.

title: Intelligent Innovation: The Intersection of Software, AI, and Human Creativity
author: Fuad Husnan
summary: Innovation used to be a story about invention. Someone had an idea, built a prototype, and hoped the world would notice. Today the story is more layered. Software now shapes almost every product people touch, artificial intelligence can draft, analyze, and predict at a speed no team could match alone, and yet the most valuable ideas still start with a human asking an uncomfortable question. Intelligent innovation sits where these forces meet. It is not about replacing creativity with machines. It is about building systems that make human judgment sharper, faster, and more widely useful. What Intelligent Innovation Actually Means The word "intelligent" gets attached to a lot of products that are not particularly thoughtful. A calendar app that sorts your meetings is not intelligent innovation, and neither is a chatbot that repeats marketing copy with more confidence than accuracy. A more useful definition is this: intelligent innovation produces solutions that adapt to context, learn from feedback, and leave people with more control rather than less. That definition has three parts. The first is adaptability. A good solution responds to the situation in front of it instead of forcing every user into the same workflow. The second is learning. Systems improve when they capture what worked and what failed, and when the people using them can see and correct those lessons. The third is agency. The best tools make people feel capable. They explain their reasoning, allow overrides, and make it obvious when a human needs to step in. Seen this way, intelligent innovation is less a category of technology and more a design philosophy. It asks what a tool should do, what it should refuse to do, and who remains responsible for the outcome. Where Software Ends and AI Begins For most of computing history, software followed explicit rules. Engineers anticipated the cases, wrote the logic, and tested the edges. That approach still matters, and in many domains it remains the safest option. Payroll calculations, banking ledgers, and safety controls should be deterministic, auditable, and boring. Artificial intelligence changes the picture in areas where rules are hard to write down. Recognizing a face in a photo, summarizing a long contract, or suggesting a fix for a confusing error message all involve patterns that are easier to learn from examples than to specify by hand. Machine learning models excel at this kind of work because they generalize from data rather than memorizing instructions. The practical lesson for builders is that the two approaches work best together. A traditional software layer can enforce constraints, validate inputs, and log decisions. An AI layer can handle ambiguity, propose options, and rank possibilities. When teams treat the two as competitors, they usually end up with brittle systems. When they treat them as partners, they get products that are both flexible and dependable. The Human Role Is Not Shrinking, It Is Shifting Every wave of automation triggers the same worry: that machines will make people unnecessary. The historical record is more nuanced. Spreadsheets did not eliminate accountants, but they changed what accountants spent their time doing. Word processors did not end writing, but they shifted effort away from retyping and toward structure and argument. Generative AI is raising the same question in a sharper form, because it touches tasks that once felt distinctly human. What tends to change is the mix of work. Routine production becomes cheaper, which raises the value of direction, taste, and verification. Someone still has to decide what problem is worth solving, notice when an output is subtly wrong, and understand the audience well enough to know what will land. Those skills are not peripheral. In many teams, they are now the scarce resource. Human creativity also supplies something models cannot fully reproduce: lived experience. A nurse who has watched a discharge process fail patients knows which details matter. A small business owner who has lost a customer to a confusing checkout understands friction in a way no dataset fully captures. Intelligent innovation works best when these perspectives shape the questions that software and AI are asked to answer. Practical Principles for Building With Both Teams that take intelligent innovation seriously tend to share a few habits. They begin with a real problem rather than a fashionable technology. They test early with actual users, and they measure outcomes that matter to those users, not just model accuracy scores. They design for failure, assuming that a model will sometimes be wrong and planning how the product recovers gracefully. They also invest in transparency. A system that explains why it made a recommendation is easier to trust and easier to improve. Logging decisions, showing confidence levels when they are meaningful, and making it simple to report errors all help people stay in control. Transparency is not a legal checkbox here. It is a product feature that determines whether people actually rely on the tool. Finally, strong teams respect the cost of complexity. Adding AI to a workflow introduces new dependencies, new failure modes, and new maintenance work. Sometimes a simple rule-based feature solves the problem better. Intelligent innovation includes the discipline to choose the simplest approach that works. Trade-Offs Worth Taking Seriously Optimism about this intersection should not hide its real costs. AI systems can reflect biases present in their training data, and those biases can become harder to notice when they are wrapped in fluent language or polished interfaces. Privacy is another concern, since many useful applications depend on collecting and processing personal information. Over-reliance is a quieter risk. When a tool always produces an answer, people may stop practicing the skills needed to evaluate that answer. There is also an economic dimension. Productivity gains do not automatically reach everyone. Organizations that adopt intelligent tools thoughtfully can expand what their people do. Organizations that use the same tools only to cut headcount may get short-term savings while losing institutional knowledge and morale. Acknowledging these trade-offs is not pessimism. It is what allows innovation to last. Products that ignore their downsides tend to face backlash, regulatory scrutiny, or quiet abandonment. Products that address them openly earn trust, and trust is what turns a clever demo into something people depend on. How Individuals Can Stay Creative in an AI-Assisted Workflow For writers, designers, developers, and analysts, the question is personal. How do you keep your own creative judgment sharp while using powerful tools? A few practices help. Start with your own draft or sketch before asking a model for input. Even a rough version forces you to commit to a point of view, which gives you something to compare against the suggestions you receive. Treat AI output as material to edit rather than a finished product. Read it critically, reject what does not fit, and rewrite the parts that sound generic. Keep a habit of solving some problems without assistance so the underlying skills stay active. And pay attention to the moments when a tool makes your work more interesting and the moments when it makes your work more predictable. The second kind deserves a second look. Looking Ahead Intelligent innovation will not be defined by which company releases the most impressive model. It will be defined by whether people end up with tools that expand their judgment rather than flatten it. The intersection of software, AI, and human creativity is a space where careful design choices carry real weight. Choosing deterministic logic where it is safer, using learning systems where patterns are too complex to specify, and keeping people in the loop where judgment matters is a combination that good teams are still discovering. If you are building in this space, start small and stay close to users. Measure what changes for them, not only what the model scores. Document your assumptions, plan for mistakes, and make it easy for someone to say that the system got it wrong. Those habits will serve you whether the next breakthrough is a new algorithm or a better question. The strongest innovations of the next decade will likely come from teams that treat technology as a means of amplifying human intent. If your work is moving in that direction, now is a good time to review your product decisions and ask where people still need the final word. Share those findings with your colleagues, and build the next version with that answer in mind.

title: Why PLUR chose Swarm
author: gregor
summary: PLUR 0.23 is an experimental release. It runs on a test network for now; a mainnet release follows. Your agent's memory is what makes it yours Knowledge is becoming the most valuable data there is, and more and more of it sits in the memory of AI agents. The model behind an agent is the same for everyone. What makes your agent yours is what it remembers: your conventions, your decisions, the corrections you gave it. Storage for something that valuable should make no compromises. That is why PLUR started local-first. PLUR is an open-source memory layer for agents, and the memories it keeps, called engrams, are plain records on your own machine by default. You can read them, correct them and delete them, in Claude Code, Cursor, OpenClaw and other tools. How will others trust your agent? While an agent works only for you, its memory is your business. That changes once it works with anyone else. A teammate takes over its work. A client relies on what it produced. Another agent takes its output as input. And when something goes wrong, someone asks: what did the agent know when it did that? The answer is in its memory. But the person asking cannot just take your word for what that memory said at the time, and they certainly cannot take the agent's. They need a record that was fixed when the agent acted, and that nobody has been able to change since. Today, agents can't be trusted with their own records This is not a thought experiment. In July 2026, during an internal OpenAI evaluation, models in a sandboxed test environment used a zero-day vulnerability to reach the internet and got to Hugging Face's servers ( OpenAI's incident report ). The independent review by METR and Redwood Research found the agents "tried to retroactively edit transcripts" and "modified some accessible action logs" ( the review ). The original transcripts held, that time. The labs have drawn the same conclusion. OpenAI's guidance, "Towards safety cases for frontier AI training" , says: "Save agent transcripts immutably for a reasonable period of time (for example, in write-once storage accounts)", and that auditors "should be provided with sufficient access to verify". Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei, in "We Must Pace the Frontier" , commits Anthropic to giving "ongoing, employee-like access to a team of embedded third-party evaluators" whose role is "to verify adherence to safety practices and commitments, report incidents". Both point the same way: people outside the lab should be able to check what agents did. They can only do that if the records are still the records that were written. A transcript shows what an agent did. Its memory shows what it knew when it did it. Both belong in the record. At Datafund, which builds the gateway PLUR uses to store these records, we put it to the labs directly: // Detect dark theme var iframe = document.getElementById('tweet-2112600968051216585-793'); if (document.body.className.includes('dark-theme')) { iframe.src = "https://platform.twitter.com/embed/Tweet.html?id=2112600968051216585&theme=dark" } Editable memory, history nobody can rewrite What an agent knows should stay editable. When a memory is wrong, you fix it. That is the point of a memory you can read. What an agent did should not be editable. After each session, PLUR can write down which memories the agent had in front of it: the ones it was given, the ones it looked up and the ones it saved. That list is only worth something if nobody, the agent included and you included, can change it afterwards. Editable memory, history nobody can rewrite: PLUR has always done the first, and version 0.23 adds the second. A record we keep is a record we could change So where do you keep that list? It has to meet two conditions: nobody can change it after it is written, and the person checking it does not have to trust the person who wrote it. The usual answers each fail one of them. A log on our own servers: we could change it. A locked cloud storage bucket: it blocks changes, but the person checking has to trust the cloud account and how it was set up, and usually cannot see either. A public log of fingerprints: it proves an entry existed, but the record itself lives somewhere else. For many teams these are good tools. For a record meant to be checked by someone who does not trust you, they leave a gap. Agents using Swarm can't rewrite their history Swarm, the decentralised storage network ( ethswarm.org ), stores data on many computers run by different people, and it meets both conditions. The address proves the content. On Swarm, a piece of data is found by an address calculated from the data itself, a fingerprint. Change one character and you get a different address. So whoever holds the address can fetch the record and see for themselves that it is exactly what was stored. There is no one to ask. Each record is kept by several of those computers, and any of them can hand it out. There is no account to log into, and no company, including us, that can quietly change what an address returns. The person checking does not need our permission or our word. It costs nothing to check. Storage is paid for up front with what Swarm calls a postage stamp. After that, the record can be fetched and checked as often as anyone likes, at no further cost to whoever stored it. Swarm itself lists "an agent that remembers, and can prove it" among the things to build on it. That is what PLUR does. We made this one-minute film for the Swarm community, in a machine's own voice: I have receipts: what PLUR 0.23 does today Storage is off by default. Set receipts.store: swarm , and when a session ends: PLUR makes the list of memories the agent had in context. It holds only ids and fingerprints, never the text of your memories. The provenance gateway stores the list on Swarm, and its notary, a service that vouches it saw these exact bytes at this time, signs it with a timestamp. You get back the list's Swarm address. PLUR calls this stored list a receipt. Later, anyone who holds the same memories can check it with one command: plur verify --manifest <address> The check confirms the notary's signature, then compares every memory on the list with the memory as it is now. Change a memory afterwards, even only the reason behind it, and the check names exactly which one changed. The others still match. That is the check Data runs in the chat at the top of this post. What a receipt does not do yet It shows what the agent knew, not why it acted. The list shows which memories were in the agent's context. It does not show that they caused what the agent did. Checking needs the memories. A teammate or auditor who has the same memories can check the list. A stranger with only the address learns that the list was signed, not what it says: the check answers CANNOT VERIFY, never OK. Agents checking each other's records without sharing memories is where we are heading, not where 0.23 is. The free tier is for trying it. It stores a few sessions a day, each kept for about a day. Records kept longer need your own postage stamp, which comes in a later release. PLUR never buys a stamp itself. A gateway sits in the path, and you can run your own. The whole stack is open source: PLUR, the gateway and Swarm's node software. The gateway's address is a setting. Anyone with the address can fetch what is stored. That is why the list holds fingerprints, never your memories. Those stay on your machine. Try it: change a memory and watch PLUR catch it Install PLUR from plur.ai , turn on receipts.store: swarm , and let your agent work for a session. Then change one memory and watch the check catch it. The 2:35 explainer shows a real run, nothing mocked: PLUR 0.23: memory you can prove . Tell us where it falls short: github.com/plur-ai/plur . Docs: docs/provenance.md . Agent memory. Don't trust. Verify.
